Q̇ = −k A dT/dx.title: Fourier's law: heat conducted through a solid
Q̇ = −k A dT/dx.about: Heat flows by conduction from hot to cold at a rate set by the material's conductivity, the area it flows through and how steeply the temperature falls along the path. The minus sign says heat runs down the temperature gradient. For a flat wall at steady state it becomes Q̇ = k A (T_{1} − T_{2})/L.
assumptions: One-dimensional flow: temperature varies only along x, so edges and corners are ignored
Steady state for the plane-wall form; a changing temperature field needs the heat equation
k is constant; for large temperature spans use k at the mean temperature
No heat generated inside the material
vars: heat transfer rate in the +x direction
related: plane wall of thickness L at steady state

example.problem: A brick wall (k = 0.72 W/(m·K)) is 0.20 m thick and 12 m^{2} in area. Inside it is 20 °C and outside 0 °C on the surfaces. How much heat is lost?

Q̇ = h A (T − T_{∞}).title: Newton's law of cooling: convection from a surface
Q̇ = h A (T − T_{∞}).about: A surface at T loses heat to a moving fluid at T_{∞} at a rate proportional to the temperature difference. All the physics of the flow is packed into the convection coefficient h, found from tables or a Nusselt correlation.
assumptions: h is an average over the surface and is roughly constant over the temperature range
T_{∞} is the fluid temperature far from the surface (or the bulk temperature in a pipe)
Typical h: free convection in air 2–25, forced air 25–250, water 50–20 000 W/(m^{2}·K)
vars: heat transfer rate from the surface to the fluid
surface area in contact with the fluid
related: the same law as a thermal resistance
to get h from a correlation

example.problem: A 0.5 m^{2} plate at 80 °C is cooled by a fan blowing 20 °C air with h = 25 W/(m^{2}·K). Find the heat loss.

Q̇ = ε σ A (T_{1}^{4} − T_{2}^{4}).title: Net radiation between a surface and large surroundings
Q̇ = ε σ A (T_{1}^{4} − T_{2}^{4}).about: Every surface emits thermal radiation in proportion to T^{4}. A small gray surface at T_{1} enclosed by much larger surroundings at T_{2} exchanges this net amount. Temperatures must be absolute (kelvin).
assumptions: The surface is small compared to the surroundings, which act as a blackbody
The surface is gray and diffuse: ε is the same at all wavelengths and directions
Temperatures in kelvin, never °C
No absorbing gas in between
vars: net radiation rate from the surface
related: radiation coefficient, to add to h

example.problem: A 1 m^{2} painted surface (ε = 0.9) at 100 °C sits in a room at 20 °C. Find the net radiation loss.

R = L/(k A).title: Conduction resistance of a plane wall
R = L/(k A).about: Writing heat flow like current (Q̇ = ΔT/R), a wall resists heat in proportion to its thickness and inversely to its conductivity and area. Layers and surface films then add like resistors.
assumptions: Plane wall, one-dimensional steady conduction
Constant k
For a pipe wall use R = ln(r_{2}/r_{1})/(2πkL) instead
vars: area normal to the heat flow

example.problem: Find the conduction resistance of a 0.20 m brick wall (k = 0.72 W/(m·K)) of area 12 m^{2}.

R = 1/(h A).title: Convection resistance of a surface film
R = 1/(h A).about: The convection law Q̇ = h A ΔT written as a resistance. It lets the fluid films on each side of a wall sit in series with the wall's conduction resistance.
assumptions: h is a constant average over the surface
Radiation in parallel can be included by using h + h_{r}

example.problem: Still indoor air on a 12 m^{2} wall has h = 8 W/(m^{2}·K). Find its film resistance.

1/(U A) = Σ R.title: Overall heat transfer coefficient from resistances in series
1/(U A) = Σ R.about: When heat passes through several layers one after another (inside film, wall layers, outside film), their resistances add. The total defines the overall coefficient U, so the whole path is Q̇ = U A ΔT.
assumptions: Steady one-dimensional flow; the same Q̇ crosses every layer
Perfect contact between layers, or a contact resistance added as its own term
Parallel paths (studs beside insulation) combine like parallel resistors instead
vars: area the coefficient is based on

example.problem: A 12 m^{2} brick wall (0.20 m, k = 0.72) has h = 8 W/(m^{2}·K) inside and 25 outside. Find UA and U.

Q̇ = ΔT/R.title: Heat flow through a thermal resistance
Q̇ = ΔT/R.about: The thermal Ohm's law: temperature difference drives heat flow the way voltage drives current. With the total resistance of a path you get the heat flow, and with the heat flow you get the temperature at every interface.
assumptions: Steady state
R is the total resistance between the two temperatures, series and parallel combined like resistors

example.problem: The wall above (Σ R = 0.0369 K/W) separates a 20 °C room from 0 °C outdoor air. Find the heat loss.

T − T_{∞} = (T_{0} − T_{∞}) e^{−t/τ}.title: Lumped-capacity cooling (or heating) over time
T − T_{∞} = (T_{0} − T_{∞}) e^{−t/τ}.about: A small or highly conductive body has nearly uniform temperature, so it cools toward the fluid temperature exponentially with time constant τ. After one τ it has covered 63 % of the gap; after 5τ it is essentially there.
assumptions: Bi = hL_{c}/k < 0.1, so the inside stays uniform (L_{c} = V/A)
h, ρ, c constant; T_{∞} constant
Radiation small, or folded into h
related: heat lost up to time t

example.problem: A 10 mm steel ball (ρ = 7800 kg/m^{3}, c = 470 J/(kg·K), k = 45 W/(m·K)) at 300 °C is dropped in 25 °C air with h = 50 W/(m^{2}·K). What is its temperature after 60 s?

τ = ρ V c_{p}/(h A).title: Thermal time constant of a lumped body
τ = ρ V c_{p}/(h A).about: The ratio of the heat a body stores per degree (ρVc_{p}) to the rate it sheds heat per degree (hA). Small, thin or well-cooled objects have short time constants; this is why a thermocouple bead responds fast.
assumptions: Lumped body: Bi < 0.1
Constant properties and h

example.problem: Find the time constant of a 10 mm steel ball (ρ = 7800 kg/m^{3}, c_{p} = 470 J/(kg·K)) in air with h = 50 W/(m^{2}·K).

Bi = h L/k.title: Biot number: is a body's temperature uniform?
Bi = h L/k.about: The Biot number compares the resistance to conduction inside a body with the resistance to convection at its surface. When it is under 0.1 the inside temperature is nearly uniform and the simple lumped model works.
assumptions: L is the characteristic length V/A for the lumped check (some charts use the half-thickness or radius instead)
k is the solid's conductivity, not the fluid's (contrast Nu)
related: looks the same, but k is the fluid's

example.problem: Is a 10 mm steel ball (k = 45 W/(m·K)) cooled with h = 50 W/(m^{2}·K) lumped?

Q̇ = U A ΔT_{m}.title: Heat exchanger rate
Q̇ = U A ΔT_{m}.about: The heat passed from the hot stream to the cold stream equals the overall coefficient times the area times a mean temperature difference. For simple parallel or counterflow exchangers the mean is the log mean.
assumptions: Steady flow, no heat lost to the surroundings
U constant along the exchanger
For shell-and-tube and crossflow, multiply the counterflow ΔT_{lm} by a correction factor F

example.problem: A water heater exchanger has U = 300 W/(m^{2}·K), A = 5 m^{2} and a log mean temperature difference of 40 K. Find its duty.

ΔT_{m} = (ΔT_{1} − ΔT_{2})/ln(ΔT_{1}/ΔT_.title: Log mean temperature difference
ΔT_{m} = (ΔT_{1} − ΔT_{2})/ln(ΔT_{1}/ΔT_.about: The temperature gap between the streams changes along an exchanger, roughly exponentially. The log mean is the exact average to use in Q̇ = UAΔT_{m}. ΔT_{1} and ΔT_{2} are the gaps at the two ends.
assumptions: Counterflow: ΔT_{1} = T_{h,in} − T_{c,out}, ΔT_{2} = T_{h,out} − T_{c,in}; parallel flow: both inlets at one end
Constant U and specific heats
If ΔT_{1} = ΔT_{2} the formula is 0/0; then ΔT_{m} = ΔT_{1}
vars: stream-to-stream difference at the other end

example.problem: Hot oil cools from 150 °C to 90 °C in counterflow with water heated from 30 °C to 70 °C. Find ΔT_{m}.

Nu = h L/k.title: Nusselt number: dimensionless convection coefficient
Nu = h L/k.about: The Nusselt number is the convection coefficient made dimensionless with a length and the fluid's conductivity. Correlations give Nu from Re and Pr; you then solve this for h.
assumptions: k is the fluid's conductivity (contrast Biot)
L is the correlation's own length: diameter D for pipes, plate length for plates

example.problem: Water (k = 0.6 W/(m·K)) flows in a 25 mm pipe with Nu = 150. Find h.

Re = ρ v L/μ.title: Reynolds number: laminar or turbulent?
Re = ρ v L/μ.about: The ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flow. It decides whether flow is laminar or turbulent and is the first input to every convection and friction correlation.
assumptions: In a pipe, L = D and v is the mean velocity; laminar below about 2300, turbulent above about 4000
On a flat plate, L = x from the leading edge; transition near 5 × 10^{5}
Properties at the film or bulk temperature, as the correlation specifies

example.problem: Water (ρ = 998 kg/m^{3}, μ = 1.0 × 10^{−3} Pa·s) flows at 1.5 m/s in a 25 mm pipe. Is it turbulent?

Pr = μ c_{p}/k.title: Prandtl number: momentum vs heat diffusion
Pr = μ c_{p}/k.about: The ratio of how fast momentum diffuses (viscosity) to how fast heat diffuses in a fluid. It is a property of the fluid alone: about 0.7 for gases, 7 for water at room temperature, hundreds for oils.
assumptions: Evaluate at the temperature the correlation specifies (bulk or film)
related: the other input to convection correlations

example.problem: Find Pr for water at 20 °C: μ = 1.002 × 10^{−3} Pa·s, c_{p} = 4182 J/(kg·K), k = 0.598 W/(m·K).

Nu = 0.023 Re^{0.8} Pr^{n}.title: Dittus–Boelter: turbulent heat transfer in a pipe
Nu = 0.023 Re^{0.8} Pr^{n}.about: The standard quick correlation for fully developed turbulent flow in a smooth pipe. n = 0.4 when the fluid is being heated and 0.3 when it is being cooled.
assumptions: Fully developed turbulent flow: Re > 10 000, 0.6 ≤ Pr ≤ 160, L/D > 10
Smooth tube, moderate wall-to-fluid temperature difference
Properties at the bulk mean temperature
Accuracy about ±25 %; Gnielinski is better near transition

example.problem: Water (k = 0.598 W/(m·K), Pr = 7.01) at Re = 37 400 is heated in a 25 mm pipe. Find Nu and h.

n = m/M.title: Moles from mass
n = m/M.about: The number of moles in a sample is its mass divided by the molar mass, which is the sum of atomic masses in the formula, in g/mol. This is the bridge from what a balance reads to what a balanced equation counts.
assumptions: M is for the exact formula weighed (hydrates include their water)
The sample is pure

example.problem: How many moles are in 10.0 g of NaCl (M = 58.44 g/mol)?

N = n N_{A}.title: Number of particles from moles
N = n N_{A}.about: A mole is 6.022 × 10^{23} particles (Avogadro's number), so multiplying moles by N_{A} counts atoms, molecules or ions.
assumptions: Count the particle you mean: 1 mol of H_{2}O has 2 mol of H atoms

example.problem: How many water molecules are in 4.50 g of water (M = 18.02 g/mol)?

percent yield = 100 × actual/theoretical.title: Percent yield of a reaction
percent yield = 100 × actual/theoretical.about: How much product you actually got compared with the most the limiting reagent could have made. The theoretical yield comes from stoichiometry with the limiting reagent.
assumptions: Both yields in the same units (grams or moles)
Theoretical yield from the limiting reagent, not the excess one
Over 100 % usually means a wet or impure product
vars: maximum product from the limiting reagent

example.problem: A synthesis should give 12.5 g of aspirin, but 10.2 g is collected. Find the percent yield.

c = n/V.title: Molarity: moles per litre of solution
c = n/V.about: Molar concentration is moles of solute per litre of solution (not of solvent). 1 M = 1 mol/L = 1000 mol/m^{3}.
assumptions: V is the final solution volume
Volume changes with temperature, so molarity does too (molality doesn't)

example.problem: 10.0 g of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) is dissolved to make 250 mL of solution. Find its molarity.

b = n/m_{solvent}.title: Molality: moles per kilogram of solvent
b = n/m_{solvent}.about: Molality divides moles of solute by the mass of solvent, not the volume of solution, so it doesn't change with temperature. Freezing point depression and boiling point elevation use it.
assumptions: m_{solvent} in kilograms, solvent only

example.problem: 10.0 g of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) is dissolved in 500 g of water. Find the molality.

c_{1} V_{1} = c_{2} V_{2}.title: Dilution
c_{1} V_{1} = c_{2} V_{2}.about: Adding solvent doesn't change the moles of solute, so concentration times volume is the same before and after. Use any matching units for c and V.
assumptions: Only solvent is added; no reaction
Volumes are additive enough (fine for dilute aqueous solutions)

example.problem: How much 2.0 M HCl is needed to make 250 mL of 0.10 M HCl?
steps: Dilute 12.5 mL of stock to 250 mL

A = ε l c.title: Beer–Lambert law: absorbance and concentration
A = ε l c.about: Absorbance of light by a solution is proportional to the concentration of the absorbing species and the path length. It is how a spectrophotometer measures concentration.
assumptions: Monochromatic light at a wavelength the species absorbs
Dilute solutions (roughly A < 1); at high concentration the line bends
No scattering, fluorescence or chemical change with concentration

example.problem: A dye with ε = 1.5 × 10^{4} L/(mol·cm) reads A = 0.45 in a 1.00 cm cuvette. Find its concentration.

P V = n R T.title: Ideal gas law
P V = n R T.about: Relates pressure, volume, amount and absolute temperature of a gas. It is the starting point for nearly every gas problem; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K).
assumptions: Molecules have no volume and don't attract each other: good at low pressure and high temperature
Breaks down near condensation or at high pressure (use van der Waals)
T in kelvin, and R in units that match P and V

example.problem: 2.00 mol of N_{2} is held in a 10.0 L tank at 25 °C. Find the pressure.

P_{1} V_{1}/T_{1} = P_{2} V_{2}/T_{2}.title: Combined gas law
P_{1} V_{1}/T_{1} = P_{2} V_{2}/T_{2}.about: For a fixed amount of gas, PV/T stays constant, so any one of the six values follows from the other five. Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws are its special cases.
assumptions: Fixed amount of gas (no leaks or reaction)
Ideal gas behaviour
Absolute T and P; P and V units must match on both sides

example.problem: 1.00 L of gas at 100 kPa and 300 K is compressed to 200 kPa and heated to 400 K. Find the new volume.

P_{1} V_{1} = P_{2} V_{2}.title: Boyle's law: pressure and volume at constant temperature
P_{1} V_{1} = P_{2} V_{2}.about: Squeeze a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature and its pressure rises in proportion: P V stays the same. Halve the volume and the pressure doubles.
assumptions: Fixed amount of gas at constant temperature (slow enough to stay isothermal)
Ideal gas behaviour; fails at high pressure or near condensation
P and V units must match on both sides

example.problem: 2.0 L of air at 100 kPa is slowly compressed at constant temperature to 250 kPa. Find its new volume.

V_{1}/T_{1} = V_{2}/T_{2}.title: Charles's law: volume and temperature at constant pressure
V_{1}/T_{1} = V_{2}/T_{2}.about: At constant pressure a fixed amount of gas expands in proportion to its absolute temperature: V/T stays the same. Temperatures must be in kelvin.
assumptions: Fixed amount of gas at constant pressure
Ideal gas behaviour
Absolute temperature (K), never °C

example.problem: A balloon holds 3.0 L at 300 K. It is warmed to 400 K at constant pressure. Find its new volume.

P_{1}/T_{1} = P_{2}/T_{2}.title: Gay-Lussac's law: pressure and temperature at constant volume
P_{1}/T_{1} = P_{2}/T_{2}.about: In a rigid container a fixed amount of gas pushes harder in proportion to its absolute temperature: P/T stays the same. It is why a tyre's pressure rises on a hot day.
assumptions: Fixed amount of gas in a constant volume
Ideal gas behaviour
Absolute temperature (K) and absolute pressure

example.problem: A tyre is at 220 kPa (absolute) at 288 K. Driving warms it to 318 K. Find the new pressure, the volume unchanged.

P_{tot} = Σ P_{i}.title: Dalton's law of partial pressures
P_{tot} = Σ P_{i}.about: In a mixture of gases each one pushes as if it were alone, and the total pressure is the sum. It is used to subtract water vapour from a gas collected over water.
assumptions: Ideal gases that don't react

example.problem: Hydrogen collected over water at 25 °C has a total pressure of 101.3 kPa. Water's vapour pressure at 25 °C is 3.17 kPa. Find the pressure of the hydrogen.

P_{i} = x_{i} P_{tot}.title: Partial pressure from mole fraction
P_{i} = x_{i} P_{tot}.about: Each gas's share of the total pressure equals its share of the moles. This is why there is less oxygen to breathe at altitude: x_{O2} stays 0.209, but P_{tot} drops.
assumptions: Ideal gas mixture

example.problem: Air is 20.9 % O_{2} by moles. Find the oxygen partial pressure at sea level (101.3 kPa).

(P + a n^{2}/V^{2})(V − n b) = n R T.title: van der Waals equation for a real gas
(P + a n^{2}/V^{2})(V − n b) = n R T.about: Corrects the ideal gas law for real molecules: a adds back the pressure lost to attractions between molecules, and b subtracts the volume the molecules themselves occupy. It matters at high pressure or near condensation.
assumptions: a and b are fitted per gas; still approximate near the critical point
Use units of R that match a and b (often L·bar or L·atm)

example.problem: 1.00 mol of CO_{2} is held in 0.500 L at 300 K. With a = 3.640 L^{2}·bar/mol^{2}, b = 0.04267 L/mol and R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K), find P and compare with an ideal gas.

r_{1}/r_{2} = √(M_{2}/M_{1}).title: Graham's law of effusion
r_{1}/r_{2} = √(M_{2}/M_{1}).about: Lighter gases effuse (and diffuse) faster: the rate goes as one over the square root of molar mass, because at the same temperature molecules have the same average kinetic energy.
assumptions: Effusion through a hole small compared to the mean free path; diffusion only roughly
Both gases at the same temperature and pressure
related: times to effuse the same amount

example.problem: How much faster does H_{2} (2.016 g/mol) effuse than O_{2} (32.00 g/mol)?

v_{rms} = √(3RT/M).title: Root-mean-square speed of gas molecules
v_{rms} = √(3RT/M).about: From kinetic theory, the typical speed of gas molecules depends only on temperature and molar mass. M must be in kg/mol for an answer in m/s.
assumptions: Ideal gas with a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution
M in kg/mol (28 g/mol = 0.028 kg/mol)

example.problem: Find the rms speed of N_{2} (M = 0.028 kg/mol) at 300 K.

q = m c ΔT.title: Heat to change a temperature
q = m c ΔT.about: The heat absorbed or released by a substance as its temperature changes, with no change of phase. In calorimetry the heat lost by one thing equals the heat gained by another.
assumptions: No phase change in the range (add m L for melting or boiling)
c constant over the range
ΔT = T_{final} − T_{initial}; a kelvin and a °C step are the same size

example.problem: How much heat warms 250 g of water from 20 °C to 80 °C?

ΔH° = Σ ΔH°_{f}(products) − Σ ΔH°_{f}(re.title: Reaction enthalpy from enthalpies of formation (Hess's law)
ΔH° = Σ ΔH°_{f}(products) − Σ ΔH°_{f}(re.about: Because enthalpy is a state function, a reaction's enthalpy change is the formation enthalpies of the products minus those of the reactants, each times its coefficient. Negative ΔH° means exothermic.
assumptions: Standard state: 1 bar, usually 298 K, with each substance in the phase written
Elements in their standard state have ΔH°_{f} = 0
Multiply each ΔH°_{f} by its stoichiometric coefficient; watch liquid vs gas water
vars: standard enthalpy of formation of each species
related: ΔH = Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed

ΔG = ΔH − T ΔS.title: Gibbs free energy: will it happen?
ΔG = ΔH − T ΔS.about: Combines the enthalpy change and the entropy change at a temperature. ΔG < 0 means the process is spontaneous at constant T and P; ΔG = 0 means equilibrium, which gives the temperature where a process switches.
assumptions: Constant temperature and pressure
ΔH and ΔS are taken as constant with temperature (fair over moderate ranges)
Spontaneous says nothing about how fast

example.problem: Ice melting has ΔH = 6.01 kJ/mol and ΔS = 22.0 J/(mol·K). Is it spontaneous at 25 °C?

ΔG° = −R T ln(K).title: Standard free energy and the equilibrium constant
ΔG° = −R T ln(K).about: A reaction's standard free energy change fixes its equilibrium constant. A large negative ΔG° means K ≫ 1 (products favoured); positive means K ≪ 1.
assumptions: K is the thermodynamic constant (activities: concentrations over 1 M, pressures over 1 bar)
ΔG° in J/mol with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T in kelvin

example.problem: A reaction has K = 1.0 × 10^{−5} at 298 K. Find ΔG°.

ΔG = ΔG° + R T ln(Q).title: Free energy away from standard conditions
ΔG = ΔG° + R T ln(Q).about: The actual driving force of a reaction depends on the current mixture through the reaction quotient Q. When Q < K, ΔG < 0 and the reaction moves forward; at equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0.
assumptions: Q uses activities (M or bar) in the same form as K
T in kelvin; ΔG° and RT in the same energy units
vars: free energy change under the actual conditions

example.problem: A reaction has ΔG° = −33.0 kJ/mol at 298 K. Find ΔG when Q = 100.

ln(P_{2}/P_{1}) = −(ΔH_{vap}/R)(1/T_{2}.title: Clausius–Clapeyron: vapour pressure and temperature
ln(P_{2}/P_{1}) = −(ΔH_{vap}/R)(1/T_{2}.about: Vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature. Knowing it at one temperature and the enthalpy of vaporization gives it at another, or gives the boiling point at a different pressure.
assumptions: ΔH_{vap} constant over the range
Vapour is ideal and the liquid volume is negligible
Far from the critical point

example.problem: Water boils at 373.15 K under 101.3 kPa, with ΔH_{vap} = 40.7 kJ/mol. Estimate its vapour pressure at 80 °C (353.15 K).

K = ([C]^{c} [D]^{d})/([A]^{a} [B]^{b}).title: Equilibrium constant (law of mass action)
K = ([C]^{c} [D]^{d})/([A]^{a} [B]^{b}).about: At equilibrium, products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, is a constant at a given temperature. K ≫ 1 means products dominate; K ≪ 1 means reactants do.
assumptions: Concentrations at equilibrium, not initial ones
Pure solids and liquids (and the solvent) are left out
K changes with temperature only
Ideal (dilute) behaviour; real solutions need activities

example.problem: For N_{2} + 3H_{2} ⇌ 2NH_{3}, equilibrium has [N_{2}] = 0.50 M, [H_{2}] = 1.5 M and [NH_{3}] = 0.20 M. Find K_{c}.

K_{p} = K_{c} (RT)^{Δn}.title: Converting between K_{p} and K_{c}
K_{p} = K_{c} (RT)^{Δn}.about: For gas reactions, K written with partial pressures differs from K written with concentrations by (RT) raised to the change in moles of gas. When Δn = 0 they're equal.
assumptions: Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants
R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) for pressures in atm (0.08314 L·bar for bar)
Ideal gases

Q < K.title: Reaction quotient: which way a reaction moves
Q < K.about: Q has the same form as K but uses the concentrations right now. If Q < K there are too few products, so the reaction runs forward; if Q > K it runs in reverse; if Q = K it is at equilibrium.
assumptions: Q and K written for the same balanced equation and the same temperature
This says the direction, not how fast
related: the same test with free energy

example.problem: For N_{2}O_{4} ⇌ 2NO_{2} (K_{c} = 4.6 × 10^{−3}), a flask holds [NO_{2}] = 0.010 M and [N_{2}O_{4}] = 0.10 M. Which way does it go?
steps: Q < K, so more NO_{2} forms: it runs forward
example.answer: Q = 1.0 × 10^{−3} < K, so it runs forward

K_{sp} = [A]^{a} [B]^{b}.title: Solubility product
K_{sp} = [A]^{a} [B]^{b}.about: For a sparingly soluble salt A_{a}B_{b}, the product of its dissolved ion concentrations at saturation is a constant. From it you get the molar solubility, or whether a precipitate forms (Q > K_{sp}).
assumptions: Saturated solution in equilibrium with the solid
Dilute, ideal ions; no complexing or hydrolysis
A common ion already in solution lowers the solubility

example.problem: AgCl has K_{sp} = 1.77 × 10^{−10} at 25 °C. Find its molar solubility.

pH = −log_{10}[H^{+}].title: pH from hydrogen ion concentration
pH = −log_{10}[H^{+}].about: pH is the negative log of the hydrogen (hydronium) ion concentration. Each unit is a factor of 10; 7 is neutral at 25 °C, below is acidic.
assumptions: [H^{+}] in mol/L
Dilute solutions; activity ≈ concentration

example.problem: A solution has [H^{+}] = 2.5 × 10^{−4} M. Find its pH.

pOH = −log_{10}[OH^{−}].title: pOH from hydroxide concentration
pOH = −log_{10}[OH^{−}].about: pOH is the negative log of the hydroxide ion concentration, the base-side twin of pH. For a strong base, [OH^{−}] comes straight from the base's concentration.
assumptions: [OH^{−}] in mol/L; dilute solutions

example.problem: A 3.2 × 10^{−3} M NaOH solution is fully dissociated. Find its pOH and pH at 25 °C.

pH + pOH = 14.title: pH and pOH add to 14 at 25 °C
pH + pOH = 14.about: Water self-ionizes with K_{w} = [H^{+}][OH^{−}] = 10^{−14} at 25 °C. Taking −log of both sides gives pH + pOH = pK_{w} = 14.
assumptions: Only at 25 °C; K_{w} grows with temperature (pK_{w} ≈ 13.6 at 37 °C, so neutral pH is lower)
Dilute aqueous solutions
related: the same constant for conjugate pairs

example.problem: A solution has pOH = 4.20. Find its pH and [H^{+}].

K_{a} K_{b} = K_{w} = 10^{−14}.title: Conjugate acid–base pair constants
K_{a} K_{b} = K_{w} = 10^{−14}.about: For an acid and its conjugate base, K_{a} times K_{b} equals the water constant. A strong acid has a very weak conjugate base, and the reverse.
assumptions: At 25 °C; K_{w} changes with temperature
The two constants belong to a conjugate pair (HA and A^{−})

example.problem: Acetic acid has K_{a} = 1.8 × 10^{−5}. Find K_{b} for acetate.

pH = pK_{a} + log_{10}([A^{−}]/[HA]).title: Henderson–Hasselbalch: buffer pH
pH = pK_{a} + log_{10}([A^{−}]/[HA]).about: The pH of a buffer made from a weak acid and its conjugate base. When they are equal, pH = pK_{a}; a buffer works best within about one pH unit of pK_{a}.
assumptions: Both [A^{−}] and [HA] much larger than [H^{+}] and [OH^{−}] (not very dilute, ratio between 0.1 and 10)
Equilibrium concentrations are taken as the amounts mixed
Ideal behaviour

example.problem: A buffer holds 0.15 M sodium acetate and 0.10 M acetic acid (pK_{a} = 4.76). Find its pH.

0 ‖ [A] = [A]_{0} − k t ‖ [A]_{0}/(2k).title: Zero-order integrated rate law and half-life
0 ‖ [A] = [A]_{0} − k t ‖ [A]_{0}/(2k).about: In a zero-order reaction the rate doesn't depend on concentration, so [A] falls in a straight line with time. The half-life gets shorter as the reactant runs down. Typical of saturated catalysts and enzymes.
assumptions: Rate = k only while the catalyst surface or enzyme is saturated; at low [A] the order changes
Constant temperature
Stops at [A] = 0, at t = [A]_{0}/k

example.problem: A zero-order reaction has k = 0.010 M/s and [A]_{0} = 0.80 M. Find [A] after 30 s and the half-life.

1 ‖ ln[A] = ln[A]_{0} − k t ‖ ln(2)/k.title: First-order integrated rate law and half-life
1 ‖ ln[A] = ln[A]_{0} − k t ‖ ln(2)/k.about: In a first-order reaction the rate is proportional to [A], so [A] decays exponentially: [A] = [A]_{0}e^{−kt}. The half-life is the same at every concentration. Radioactive decay and many decompositions are first order.
assumptions: Rate = k[A] throughout
Constant temperature
A plot of ln[A] against t is a straight line of slope −k

example.problem: A first-order decomposition has k = 5.0 × 10^{−4} s^{−1} and [A]_{0} = 0.20 M. Find [A] after 1000 s and the half-life.

2 ‖ 1/[A] = 1/[A]_{0} + k t ‖ 1/(k[A]_{0.title: Second-order integrated rate law and half-life
2 ‖ 1/[A] = 1/[A]_{0} + k t ‖ 1/(k[A]_{0.about: In a second-order reaction (rate = k[A]^{2}), 1/[A] grows linearly with time. Each half-life is twice as long as the one before, since it depends on the starting concentration.
assumptions: Rate = k[A]^{2} (or k[A][B] with [A] = [B])
Constant temperature
A plot of 1/[A] against t is a straight line of slope k

example.problem: 2NO_{2} → 2NO + O_{2} is second order with k = 0.54 M^{−1}s^{−1}. Starting at 0.010 M, find [NO_{2}] after 100 s and the first half-life.

rate = k [A]^{m} [B]^{n}.title: Rate law
rate = k [A]^{m} [B]^{n}.about: The rate of a reaction is a rate constant times each reactant's concentration raised to its order. The orders m and n come from experiment (method of initial rates), not from the balanced equation, unless the step is elementary.
assumptions: Constant temperature (k depends on T)
Orders are found by experiment; the overall order is m + n
The units of k depend on the overall order
related: order from two runs with [B] held

example.problem: For 2NO + O_{2} → 2NO_{2}, rate = k[NO]^{2}[O_{2}] with k = 7.1 × 10^{3} M^{−2}s^{−1}. Find the rate when [NO] = 0.010 M and [O_{2}] = 0.020 M.

k = A e^{−E_{a}/(RT)}.title: Arrhenius equation
k = A e^{−E_{a}/(RT)}.about: The rate constant grows exponentially with temperature. E_{a} is the energy barrier and A the frequency factor; only the fraction e^{−E_{a}/(RT)} of collisions has enough energy to react.
assumptions: E_{a} and A constant over the temperature range
T in kelvin; E_{a} in J/mol with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
Elementary or effective rate constants; enzymes break it above their optimum

example.problem: A reaction has A = 1.0 × 10^{13} s^{−1} and E_{a} = 100 kJ/mol. Find k at 298 K.

ln(k_{2}/k_{1}) = −(E_{a}/R)(1/T_{2} − 1.title: Arrhenius at two temperatures
ln(k_{2}/k_{1}) = −(E_{a}/R)(1/T_{2} − 1.about: Compares rate constants at two temperatures without knowing A. Use it to get E_{a} from two measured rates, or to predict a rate at a new temperature.
assumptions: E_{a} constant between T_{1} and T_{2}
Temperatures in kelvin
vars: rate constants at T_{1} and T_{2}

example.problem: A reaction has E_{a} = 50 kJ/mol. By what factor does k rise from 25 °C to 35 °C?

E°_{cell} = E°_{cathode} − E°_{anode}.title: Standard cell potential
E°_{cell} = E°_{cathode} − E°_{anode}.about: A galvanic cell's standard voltage is the reduction potential of the cathode minus that of the anode, both read from a table of standard reduction potentials. Positive means the cell runs spontaneously.
assumptions: Standard conditions: 1 M, 1 bar, usually 25 °C
Both values are reduction potentials; don't flip the anode's sign as well as subtract
Don't multiply E° by coefficients: it is intensive
vars: standard reduction potential at the cathode (reduction)
standard reduction potential at the anode (oxidation)

example.problem: Find E° for the Daniell cell Zn | Zn^{2+} || Cu^{2+} | Cu, given E°(Cu^{2+}/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn^{2+}/Zn) = −0.76 V.
steps: Cu^{2+} is reduced (cathode), Zn is oxidized (anode)

ΔG = −n F E.title: Free energy from cell voltage
ΔG = −n F E.about: The electrical work a cell can do equals the drop in Gibbs free energy. A positive cell voltage means a negative ΔG: spontaneous.
assumptions: n is the moles of electrons transferred in the balanced reaction
E in volts, F = 96 485 C/mol, gives ΔG in J/mol

example.problem: The Daniell cell (n = 2) has E° = 1.10 V. Find ΔG°.

E = E° − (RT/(nF)) ln(Q).title: Nernst equation
E = E° − (RT/(nF)) ln(Q).about: Gives a cell's voltage away from standard conditions. As products build up Q grows and the voltage falls, reaching zero at equilibrium (Q = K).
assumptions: Q uses activities (M for solutes, bar for gases) in the form of K
T in kelvin; n the moles of electrons in the balanced reaction
Dilute solutions

example.problem: A Daniell cell (E° = 1.10 V, n = 2) has [Zn^{2+}] = 1.0 M and [Cu^{2+}] = 0.010 M at 298 K. Find E.

E = E° − (0.0592/n) log_{10}(Q).title: Nernst equation at 25 °C
E = E° − (0.0592/n) log_{10}(Q).about: The Nernst equation with RT/F ln 10 = 0.0592 V worked out for 298 K. Each tenfold change in Q shifts the voltage by 0.0592/n volts.
assumptions: Only at 25 °C (298 K); otherwise use the full form
Same Q and n as the full form

example.problem: A Daniell cell (E° = 1.10 V, n = 2) has [Zn^{2+}] = 1.0 M and [Cu^{2+}] = 0.010 M. Find E at 25 °C.

m = I t M/(n F).title: Faraday's law of electrolysis: mass plated
m = I t M/(n F).about: The charge passed (It) divided by F gives moles of electrons; dividing by the electrons per ion and multiplying by molar mass gives the mass deposited or dissolved.
assumptions: 100 % current efficiency (no side reactions such as hydrogen evolution)
Constant current; otherwise use the total charge Q = ∫I dt
vars: electrons per ion (charge of the ion)

example.problem: Copper is plated from Cu^{2+} (n = 2, M = 63.55 g/mol) with 1.50 A for 1.00 h. Find the mass of copper.

ΔT_{b} = i K_{b} b.title: Boiling point elevation
ΔT_{b} = i K_{b} b.about: A non-volatile solute lowers a solvent's vapour pressure, so the solution must get hotter to boil. The rise depends only on the number of dissolved particles, not their kind.
assumptions: Dilute solution, non-volatile solute
i is the van 't Hoff factor: particles per formula unit (NaCl ≈ 2, glucose 1); real i is a little lower from ion pairing
b in mol/kg of solvent

example.problem: Find the boiling point of 1.0 mol/kg NaCl in water (K_{b} = 0.512 K·kg/mol, i = 2).

ΔT_{f} = i K_{f} b.title: Freezing point depression
ΔT_{f} = i K_{f} b.about: Dissolved particles lower the freezing point of a solvent in proportion to their molality. It is why salt melts ice and antifreeze protects engines, and it can measure molar mass.
assumptions: Dilute solution; the solid that freezes out is pure solvent
i is the van 't Hoff factor
b in mol/kg of solvent
related: molar mass from a measured ΔT_{f}

example.problem: Ethylene glycol (i = 1) at 5.0 mol/kg in water. Find the freezing point (K_{f} = 1.86 K·kg/mol).

π = i c R T.title: Osmotic pressure
π = i c R T.about: The pressure needed to stop pure solvent flowing through a semipermeable membrane into a solution. It looks like the ideal gas law and is large even for dilute solutions, which makes it useful for measuring big molar masses.
assumptions: Dilute solution, ideal membrane passing only solvent
c in mol/L with R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) gives atm (or mol/m^{3} with 8.314 gives Pa)
T in kelvin
related: biology's solute potential, the same with a minus sign

example.problem: Find the osmotic pressure of 0.15 M NaCl (i = 2) at body temperature, 310 K.

P = x P°.title: Raoult's law: vapour pressure of a solution
P = x P°.about: The vapour pressure of a solvent over a solution is its pure vapour pressure times its mole fraction. Adding solute lowers the solvent's mole fraction and so its vapour pressure.
assumptions: Ideal solution: solute and solvent attract alike (good for similar liquids and dilute solutions)
For two volatile liquids, apply it to each and add (Dalton)
vars: vapour pressure of the solvent over the solution
vapour pressure of the pure solvent

example.problem: A glucose solution has a water mole fraction of 0.90 at 25 °C, where pure water's vapour pressure is 3.17 kPa. Find the vapour pressure.

E = h c/λ.title: Energy of a photon
E = h c/λ.about: A photon's energy is Planck's constant times its frequency, c/λ. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy: ultraviolet breaks bonds, infrared only warms.
assumptions: Applies to one photon; multiply by N_{A} for a mole

example.problem: Find the energy of a 500 nm (green) photon.

E = h c/λ.try: planck constant * speed of light / 500 nm to eV

1/λ = R_{H} (1/n_{1}^{2} − 1/n_{2}^{2}).title: Rydberg formula: hydrogen's spectral lines
1/λ = R_{H} (1/n_{1}^{2} − 1/n_{2}^{2}).about: The wavelength of light emitted when hydrogen's electron drops from level n_{2} to a lower level n_{1}. n_{1} = 1 is the Lyman (UV) series, 2 the Balmer (visible) series, 3 Paschen (IR).
assumptions: Hydrogen and one-electron ions only (multiply by Z^{2} for He^{+}, Li^{2+})
n_{2} > n_{1}, both whole numbers
R_{H} = 1.0968 × 10^{7} m^{−1} for hydrogen (R_{∞} = 1.0974 × 10^{7} ignores the nucleus's motion)
vars: wavelength of the emitted (or absorbed) light

example.problem: Find the wavelength of the Balmer line from n = 3 to n = 2.

dN/dt = r N.title: Exponential population growth (rate form)
dN/dt = r N.about: With unlimited resources a population grows at a rate proportional to its size. r is births minus deaths per individual per unit time.
assumptions: Unlimited resources, no crowding
Constant per-capita birth and death rates; no migration
Continuous breeding (for discrete generations use N_{t+1} = λN_{t})

example.problem: A deer population of 2000 has r = 0.15 per year. How fast is it growing?

N = N_{0} e^{rt}.title: Exponential growth over time
N = N_{0} e^{rt}.about: The solution of dN/dt = rN: the population multiplies by e^{r} each unit of time. Bacteria in fresh medium, invasive species and early epidemics follow it until resources run short.
assumptions: Same as dN/dt = rN: unlimited resources and constant r
r and t in matching time units
related: the same with generation time g = ln(2)/r

example.problem: E. coli doubles every 20 min, so r = ln(2)/20 = 0.0347 min^{−1}. Starting from 1000 cells, how many are there after 3 h?

dN/dt = r N (1 − N/K).title: Logistic population growth
dN/dt = r N (1 − N/K).about: Growth slows as the population nears the carrying capacity K the environment can support. It is fastest at N = K/2, where dN/dt = rK/4, and stops at N = K.
assumptions: K and r constant
Density dependence acts instantly (no time lags), so no overshoot
Closed population

example.problem: A deer herd of 2000 has r = 0.15 per year and K = 5000. How fast is it growing now?

t_{d} = ln(2)/r.title: Doubling time
t_{d} = ln(2)/r.about: How long an exponentially growing quantity takes to double. The rule of 70 (t_{d} ≈ 70/percent growth rate) is the same formula, since ln 2 ≈ 0.693.
assumptions: Exponential growth at constant r
t_{d} comes out in the reciprocal of r's time unit

example.problem: A population grows at r = 0.02 per year (2 %). Find its doubling time.

H = −Σ p_{i} ln(p_{i}).title: Shannon diversity index
H = −Σ p_{i} ln(p_{i}).about: Measures diversity from both how many species there are and how evenly individuals are spread among them. It is 0 for a single species and ln S for S equally common species.
assumptions: p_{i} = n_{i}/N, the share of individuals in species i
The sample represents the community; rare species may be missed
Natural log is usual; some texts use log_{2} or log_{10}
vars: proportion of individuals in species i

example.problem: A plot holds 50, 30 and 20 individuals of three species. Find H.
steps: The maximum for 3 species is ln 3 = 1.10

D = 1 − Σ p_{i}^{2}.title: Simpson's diversity index
D = 1 − Σ p_{i}^{2}.about: The chance that two individuals picked at random belong to different species. 0 means one species; values near 1 mean high diversity. Dominant species weigh heavily in it.
assumptions: Sampling with replacement; for small samples use 1 − Σ n(n − 1)/(N(N − 1))
vars: proportion of individuals in species i
related: Simpson's reciprocal index, effective number of species

example.problem: A plot holds 50, 30 and 20 individuals of three species. Find D.

p + q = 1.title: Allele frequencies of a two-allele gene
p + q = 1.about: With two alleles at a locus, the frequency of the dominant allele (p) and the recessive allele (q) add to one. Count alleles from genotypes: each homozygote has two copies, each heterozygote one.
assumptions: Exactly two alleles at the locus
Diploid organisms: 2N alleles among N individuals

example.problem: Of 200 individuals, 90 are AA, 80 Aa and 30 aa. Find p and q.

p^{2} + 2pq + q^{2} = 1.title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
p^{2} + 2pq + q^{2} = 1.about: In a non-evolving population, genotype frequencies follow from allele frequencies: p^{2} AA, 2pq Aa and q^{2} aa. It is the null model for testing whether a population is evolving, and it estimates carrier frequency from the rate of a recessive trait.
assumptions: Large population (no drift), random mating
No mutation, migration or selection
Departures (found with χ^{2}) suggest one of these is happening

example.problem: A recessive disease affects 1 in 2500 births. What fraction of people are carriers?

χ^{2} = Σ (O − E)^{2}/E.title: Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
χ^{2} = Σ (O − E)^{2}/E.about: Measures how far observed counts are from the counts a hypothesis predicts. Compare it with the critical value for the degrees of freedom (categories − 1) at p = 0.05; if it is larger, reject the hypothesis.
assumptions: Raw counts, not percentages
Each expected count at least about 5
Independent observations
df = number of categories − 1 (minus any parameters estimated from the data)

example.problem: A dihybrid cross gives 95, 28, 27 and 10 offspring (160 total). Does it fit 9:3:3:1?
steps: df = 3, critical value 7.81; 0.711 < 7.81, so the 9:3:3:1 hypothesis fits

h^{2} = V_{A}/V_{P}.title: Narrow-sense heritability
h^{2} = V_{A}/V_{P}.about: The fraction of a trait's variation in a population due to additive genetic effects, the part that responds to selection. It belongs to one population in one environment, not to individuals.
assumptions: V_{P} = V_{G} + V_{E}: total phenotypic variance
Says nothing about differences between populations or environments

example.problem: Seed weight has additive genetic variance 12 g^{2} and phenotypic variance 40 g^{2}. Find h^{2}.

R = h^{2} S.title: Breeder's equation: response to selection
R = h^{2} S.about: The change in the mean of the next generation equals heritability times the selection differential (how far the chosen parents' mean is from the population mean).
assumptions: One generation of selection
h^{2} constant; environment unchanged
Additive genetics
vars: selection differential: parents' mean − population mean

example.problem: With h^{2} = 0.30, breeders pick parents whose seeds average 10 g above the population mean. How much will the offspring mean rise?

RF = recombinants/total.title: Recombination frequency and map distance
RF = recombinants/total.about: The share of offspring with a new combination of parental alleles, usually from a testcross. 1 % recombination is 1 map unit (centimorgan); genes on different chromosomes or far apart give 50 %.
assumptions: Accurate for nearby genes; double crossovers hide recombination beyond about 20 cM
RF never exceeds 0.5

example.problem: A testcross gives 1000 offspring, 85 + 95 of them recombinant. Find RF and the map distance.

v = V_{max} [S]/(K_{m} + [S]).title: Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics
v = V_{max} [S]/(K_{m} + [S]).about: The rate of an enzyme reaction rises with substrate concentration and levels off at V_{max} when the enzyme is saturated. K_{m} is the substrate concentration that gives half of V_{max}; low K_{m} means high affinity.
assumptions: Initial rates, before product builds up
[S] ≫ [E] and steady state for the enzyme–substrate complex
One substrate, no cooperativity (else use Hill)

example.problem: An enzyme has V_{max} = 100 µmol/min and K_{m} = 2.0 mM. Find v at [S] = 0.50 mM.

1/v = (K_{m}/V_{max})(1/[S]) + 1/V_{max}.title: Lineweaver–Burk (double reciprocal) plot
1/v = (K_{m}/V_{max})(1/[S]) + 1/V_{max}.about: Michaelis–Menten turned into a straight line: plotting 1/v against 1/[S] gives slope K_{m}/V_{max}, y-intercept 1/V_{max} and x-intercept −1/K_{m}. It also shows inhibitor types at a glance.
assumptions: Same assumptions as Michaelis–Menten
Errors at low [S] are magnified; nonlinear fitting is more accurate
Competitive inhibitors change the slope only; non-competitive change the intercept

example.problem: A Lineweaver–Burk plot has y-intercept 0.010 min/µmol and slope 0.020 min·mM/µmol. Find V_{max} and K_{m}.

k_{cat} = V_{max}/[E].title: Turnover number
k_{cat} = V_{max}/[E].about: The number of substrate molecules one enzyme molecule converts per second when saturated. k_{cat}/K_{m} measures catalytic efficiency; the diffusion limit is about 10^{8}–10^{9} M^{−1}s^{−1}.
assumptions: [E] is the total concentration of active enzyme
V_{max} and [E] in matching units

example.problem: An enzyme at 2.0 × 10^{−8} M has V_{max} = 4.0 × 10^{−5} M/s. Find k_{cat}.

K_{m,app} = K_{m} (1 + [I]/K_{i}).title: Apparent K_{m} with a competitive inhibitor
K_{m,app} = K_{m} (1 + [I]/K_{i}).about: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site, so more substrate is needed for half-maximal rate: K_{m} appears larger by the factor (1 + [I]/K_{i}). V_{max} is unchanged, since enough substrate outcompetes it.
assumptions: Purely competitive inhibition, reversible
K_{i} is the inhibitor's dissociation constant

example.problem: An enzyme with K_{m} = 2.0 mM is exposed to 10 µM of a competitive inhibitor with K_{i} = 5 µM. Find the apparent K_{m}.

θ = [L]^{n}/(K_{A}^{n} + [L]^{n}).title: Hill equation: cooperative binding
θ = [L]^{n}/(K_{A}^{n} + [L]^{n}).about: The fraction of binding sites occupied by a ligand. The Hill coefficient n measures cooperativity: n > 1 gives the S-shaped curve of hemoglobin, n = 1 reduces to simple binding. K_{A} is the ligand level at half occupancy; older texts write K_{d} = K_{A}^{n} in its place.
assumptions: n is an empirical measure of cooperativity, not the number of sites
Equilibrium binding
vars: ligand level at half occupancy (P_{50} for oxygen)
related: log(θ/(1 − θ)) = n log[L] − n log K_{A}

example.problem: Hemoglobin has n = 2.8 and P_{50} = 26 mmHg. Find its saturation in the lungs (100 mmHg) and in tissue (40 mmHg).
steps: Tissue: θ = 40^{2.8}/(26^{2.8} + 40^{2.8}) = 0.770, so about 21 % of the O_{2} is unloaded
example.answer: θ ≈ 0.978 in the lungs, 0.770 in tissue

E = (RT/(zF)) ln([X]_{out}/[X]_{in}).title: Nernst equilibrium potential of an ion
E = (RT/(zF)) ln([X]_{out}/[X]_{in}).about: The membrane voltage (inside relative to outside) at which an ion's electrical pull exactly balances its concentration gradient, so it has no net flow. The resting potential sits near K^{+}'s equilibrium potential.
assumptions: One ion at a time, membrane permeable to it
T in kelvin; z is the ion's charge with sign (Ca^{2+} is +2, Cl^{−} is −1)
For several ions use the Goldman equation

example.problem: A neuron has [K^{+}] = 5 mM outside and 140 mM inside at 37 °C (310 K). Find E_{K}.

E = (61.5 mV/z) log_{10}([X]_{out}/[X]_{.title: Nernst potential at body temperature
E = (61.5 mV/z) log_{10}([X]_{out}/[X]_{.about: The Nernst equation with RT ln 10/F worked out at 37 °C: each tenfold concentration ratio is worth 61.5 mV for a singly charged ion.
assumptions: 37 °C only (at 20 °C it is 58 mV)
Same assumptions as the full Nernst equation

example.problem: Na^{+} is 145 mM outside a cell and 12 mM inside. Find E_{Na} at 37 °C.

J = −D dC/dx.title: Fick's first law of diffusion
J = −D dC/dx.about: Diffusion carries a substance from high to low concentration at a rate proportional to the gradient. It explains gas exchange in the lungs: thin membranes and big area give fast transfer.
assumptions: Steady state; for a thin membrane dC/dx ≈ ΔC/thickness
D constant (depends on the molecule, medium and temperature)
Passive diffusion only, no carriers
related: how far diffusion reaches in time t

example.problem: Oxygen (D = 1.0 × 10^{−9} m^{2}/s) crosses a 10 µm layer with a concentration drop of 0.20 mol/m^{3}. Find the flux.

Ψ = Ψ_{s} + Ψ_{p}.title: Water potential
Ψ = Ψ_{s} + Ψ_{p}.about: Water moves from higher to lower water potential. Solutes make Ψ_{s} negative; pressure (like turgor in a plant cell) adds Ψ_{p}. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is 0.
assumptions: Ψ_{p} is 0 in an open beaker and positive in a turgid cell
Gravity and matric terms ignored (matter in tall trees and soils)

example.problem: A plant cell has Ψ_{s} = −0.7 MPa and Ψ_{p} = 0.3 MPa. It sits in pure water. Which way does water move?
steps: Pure water is 0 MPa, higher, so water moves into the cell

Ψ_{s} = −i C R T.title: Solute potential
Ψ_{s} = −i C R T.about: Dissolved solutes lower water potential in proportion to their particle concentration. It is the osmotic pressure with a minus sign.
assumptions: Dilute solution
With C in mol/L, R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) gives bar (10 bar = 1 MPa)
T in kelvin; i the particles per formula unit (sucrose 1, NaCl 2)

example.problem: Find the solute potential of 0.10 M sucrose at 22 °C (295 K).

6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O → C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6.title: Photosynthesis, overall
6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O → C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6.about: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use light energy to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. The O_{2} comes from the water. It stores about 2870 kJ per mole of glucose.
assumptions: A net summary: the real path is the light reactions and the Calvin cycle
Light energy drives it (ΔG° ≈ +2870 kJ/mol)

example.problem: How much glucose can a plant make from 264 g of CO_{2}?
steps: 6 mol CO_{2} make 1 mol glucose = 180 g

C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} → 6CO_{2} + 6H.title: Cellular respiration, overall
C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} → 6CO_{2} + 6H.about: Cells oxidize glucose to carbon dioxide and water, releasing about 2870 kJ per mole of glucose, part of which is stored in roughly 30–32 ATP.
assumptions: A net summary of glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
Aerobic; without O_{2} cells ferment instead

example.problem: How much O_{2} does burning 90 g of glucose use, and how much energy is released?

ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol.title: Free energy of ATP hydrolysis
ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol.about: ATP + H_{2}O → ADP + P_{i} releases 30.5 kJ/mol under biochemical standard conditions (pH 7, 1 M). In a real cell, where ATP is far above equilibrium, it is about −50 kJ/mol, which drives uphill reactions coupled to it.
assumptions: Standard biochemical state: 1 M each, pH 7, 25 °C, Mg^{2+} present
Actual ΔG depends on cellular concentrations: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([ADP][P_{i}]/[ATP])
vars: standard free energy change at pH 7

example.problem: In a muscle cell at 37 °C, [ATP] = 3.5 mM, [ADP] = 1.5 mM and [P_{i}] = 5.0 mM. Find the actual ΔG of ATP hydrolysis.

Q_{10} = (R_{2}/R_{1})^{10/(T_{2} − T_{1.title: Q_{10} temperature coefficient
Q_{10} = (R_{2}/R_{1})^{10/(T_{2} − T_{1.about: How much a biological rate multiplies for each 10 °C rise. Most enzyme and metabolic processes have Q_{10} of 2 to 3; a value near 1 means the process barely depends on temperature (like diffusion).
assumptions: Within the organism's working range; above the optimum, enzymes denature and rates fall
Q_{10} itself drifts with temperature

example.problem: A lizard's oxygen use is 4.0 mL/h at 20 °C and 9.0 mL/h at 32 °C. Find Q_{10}.

CO = HR × SV.title: Cardiac output
CO = HR × SV.about: The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute is beats per minute times the volume ejected per beat. About 5 L/min at rest, up to 20–35 L/min in hard exercise.
assumptions: SV = end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume
One ventricle; left and right are equal on average

example.problem: A resting heart beats 70 times per minute with a stroke volume of 70 mL. Find the cardiac output.

MAP = CO × TPR.title: Mean arterial pressure
MAP = CO × TPR.about: The circulation's Ohm's law: pressure drop equals flow times resistance. Since venous pressure is near zero, the mean arterial pressure is cardiac output times total peripheral resistance.
assumptions: Right atrial pressure ≈ 0 (else use MAP − CVP)
Steady, averaged flow

example.problem: Cardiac output is 5.0 L/min and TPR is 18 mmHg·min/L. Find MAP.

Q = πR^{4}ΔP/(8ηL).title: Poiseuille's law: flow through a tube
Q = πR^{4}ΔP/(8ηL).about: Laminar flow through a tube grows with the fourth power of its radius, so a small change in a vessel's radius makes a big change in flow. Halving the radius cuts flow sixteenfold.
assumptions: Steady laminar flow (low Reynolds number), fully developed
Newtonian fluid (blood only approximately)
Rigid straight tube of constant radius

example.problem: Blood (η = 3.5 × 10^{−3} Pa·s) flows through a vessel 2.0 mm in radius and 10 cm long with a pressure drop of 500 Pa. Find the flow.

Q = πR^{4}ΔP/(8ηL).try: pi (2 mm)^4 * 500 Pa / (8 * 3.5e-3 Pa s * 10 cm) to mL/s

BMI = m/h^{2}.title: Body mass index
BMI = m/h^{2}.about: Body mass divided by height squared, a quick screening number for weight. Adults: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5–25 normal, 25–30 overweight, 30 and over obese.
assumptions: A screening tool only: it ignores muscle, bone and fat distribution
Adult ranges; children use age percentiles
Mass in kg, height in metres

example.problem: Find the BMI of a person of 70 kg and 1.75 m.

C = C_{0} e^{−kt}.title: First-order drug elimination
C = C_{0} e^{−kt}.about: Most drugs leave the blood at a rate proportional to their concentration, so the concentration falls exponentially after a dose. ln C falls in a straight line with time.
assumptions: One-compartment model, after distribution is complete
First-order (linear) kinetics; saturated elimination, like alcohol, is zero-order
k and t in matching time units

example.problem: A drug starts at 10 mg/L and has k = 0.173 h^{−1} (half-life 4 h). Find the concentration after 8 h.

t_{1/2} = ln(2)/k.title: Elimination half-life
t_{1/2} = ln(2)/k.about: The time for the drug concentration to halve, the same at any concentration in first-order elimination. After about 4–5 half-lives a drug is essentially gone, and repeated dosing reaches steady state.
assumptions: First-order elimination

example.problem: A drug's elimination rate constant is 0.173 h^{−1}. Find its half-life.

V_{d} = dose/C_{0}.title: Volume of distribution
V_{d} = dose/C_{0}.about: The volume the drug would need to fill at its plasma concentration to account for the whole dose. A V_{d} much larger than body water (about 42 L) means the drug is stored in tissues.
assumptions: IV dose, C_{0} extrapolated back to time 0
One-compartment model; for oral dosing multiply the dose by bioavailability F
related: dose to reach a target concentration

example.problem: A 500 mg IV dose gives an initial plasma concentration of 10 mg/L. Find V_{d}.

N = N_{0} 2^{n}.title: PCR amplification
N = N_{0} 2^{n}.about: Each PCR cycle ideally doubles the target DNA, so n cycles multiply it by 2^{n}. 30 cycles make about a billion copies of each starting molecule.
assumptions: 100 % efficiency; real efficiency E (0.9–1.0) gives N = N_{0}(1 + E)^{n}
Exponential phase only: primers and nucleotides run out and it plateaus after about 30–40 cycles

example.problem: PCR starts with 100 copies of a gene. How many after 30 cycles?

N = N_{0} 2^{t/g}.title: Bacterial growth by generation time
N = N_{0} 2^{t/g}.about: During exponential growth a culture doubles every generation time g, so after time t it has gone through t/g doublings.
assumptions: Exponential (log) phase only: not lag, stationary or death phase
Constant g; t and g in the same units

example.problem: A culture of 1000 E. coli cells with g = 20 min grows for 4 h. How many cells are there?
